title: Section 251 — Offering gift or restoration of property in consideration of screening offender

content.overview: BNS s. 251 — Offering gift or restoration of property in consideration of screening offender.
content.study:
Introduction and meaning
Offering gift or restoration of property in consideration of screening offender. Historical concordance: IPC 215. For conduct governed by the BNS, cite BNS section 251; the IPC reference is historical concordance.
In student language: BNS s. 251 is the rule on “Offering gift or restoration of property in consideration of screening offender”. The section provides that whoever gives or causes, or offers or agrees to give or cause, any gratification to any person, or restores or causes the restoration of any property to any person, in consideration of that person’s concealing an offence, or of his screening any person from legal punishment for any offence, or of his not proceeding against any person for the purpose of bringing him to legal punishment shall,–. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Why this is asked
Criminal law arguments turn on statutory ingredients. BNS s. 251 exists so that “Offering gift or restoration of property in consideration of screening offender” has a closed legal test in Chapter XIV — Of False Evidence and Offences Against Public Justice. An authoritative analysis defines the concept, lists every ingredient, walks the statutory illustrations, states exceptions, and applies the test methodically to facts.
Chapter setting: Perjury, screening, harbouring, false charge, and failing to appear on a bond.

The provision in detail
251. Whoever gives or causes, or offers or agrees to give or cause, any gratification to any person, or restores or causes the restoration of any property to any person, in consideration of that person’s concealing an offence, or of his screening any person from legal punishment for any offence, or of his not proceeding against any person for the purpose of bringing him to legal punishment shall,–

(a) if the offence is punishable with death, be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine;

(b) if the offence is punishable with imprisonment for life or with imprisonment which may extend to ten years, be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, and shall also be liable to fine;

(c) if the offence is punishable with imprisonment not extending to ten years, be punished with imprisonment of the description provided for the offence for a term which may extend to one-fourth part of the longest term of imprisonment provided for the offence, or with fine, or with both

Essential ingredients
1. Whoever gives or causes, or offers or agrees to give or cause, any gratification to any person, or restores or causes the restoration of any property to any person, in consideration of that person’s concealing an offence, or of his screening any person from legal punishment for any offence, or of his not proceeding against any person for the purpose of bringing him to legal punishment shall,–
2. (a) if the offence is punishable with death, be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine;
3. (b) if the offence is punishable with imprisonment for life or with imprisonment which may extend to ten years, be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, and shall also be liable to fine;
4. (c) if the offence is punishable with imprisonment not extending to ten years, be punished with imprisonment of the description provided for the offence for a term which may extend to one-fourth part of the longest term of imprisonment provided for the offence, or with fine, or with both

Exceptions, limitations and provisos
Exception.—The provisions of this section and section 250 do not extend to any case in which the offence may lawfully be compounded

enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 251 constitutes a key component of Chapter XIV (Of False Evidence and Offences against Public Justice) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, addressing offering gift or restoration of property in consideration of screening offender. The provision balances personal liberty with public interest and social order. The prosecution must establish every statutory element beyond reasonable doubt: the specified actus reus, the requisite mens rea, and any relevant statutory circumstances. Modern judicial interpretation emphasizes substantive fairness, proportionality in sentencing, and adherence to constitutional safeguards. Where statutory exceptions or provisos are attached to the section, the accused must establish facts bringing the case within such provisions under evidentiary standards.
examples: Teaching example (Standard application): An individual intentionally commits acts satisfying the statutory formula of offering gift or restoration of property in consideration of screening offender under Section 251 without lawful authority. The individual is liable under BNS s. 251.

Teaching example (Absence of mens rea / Lawful exception): A person acts in good faith or without the requisite statutory mental element under circumstances recognized by law. The essential ingredients of Section 251 are not satisfied; no penal liability attaches.
distinctions: Section 251 vs General Attempt: Section 251 penalizes the substantive conduct specified in Chapter XIV; inchoate attempts without specific provisions fall under the general attempt provisions.

Section 251 vs Cognate Chapter Offences: Liability under Section 251 is distinguished by its specific mental threshold and the particular legal interest protected under Of False Evidence and Offences against Public Justice.
